outputs.L2:
On South Street I encountered a tall man, with a jittery shark’s tooth dangling from a chain around his neck. His eyes seemed to push outward behind green lenses—whether the glasses were green or the saloon lights turned them that color, they glittered green. Those eyes moved past you, as if they had forgotten to meet yours, or as if they had abandoned you somewhere back along the street.

From the coin-operated piano came the uneven tune of “Stamboul Nights,” set loose by someone’s nickel, and the song drifted out: “O Stamboul Rose—dreams weave the rose!” He talked in low, oceanic mutters about Leviathan, while rum turned Plato loose inside our skulls.

“It’s the S.S. Ala—Antwerp,” he said. “Now don’t forget, kid—wake me at three. She leaves right on schedule. I’m not much use with time anymore. I keep weak-eyed watches and sometimes doze off—” His thin, knuckled hands began tapping out a rhythm. “Once I was on a whaler. I ought to be able to keep time and get past it. I’m a Democrat. I know what time it is. No—I don’t want to know what time it is. That cursed white Arctic murdered time for me . . .”

“O Stamboul Rose”—the drums seemed to braid the sound.

“I operated a donkey engine down on the Panama Canal. Got sick of that. Afterward it was Yucatan, peddling kitchen goods—beads. Have you ever seen Popocatepetl? A birdless crater, ash drifting down from its mouth? Then back to the coast again . . .”

“Rose of Stamboul, O coral Queen”—the song teased out broken remains of ruined cities, endless corridors and galleries, lava hollowed and chewed by water, stone snarling green, while the drums deepened and swallowed the sound.
outputs.L3:
In South Street, the narrator encounters a tall, nervous man whose appearance immediately sets him apart from the dim, shifting crowd around him. His eyes have a strange greenish tinge, giving his face an unsettled, almost sea-haunted look, and around his neck hangs a chain of shark’s teeth that adds to his striking, slightly menacing presence. He seems both vivid and insubstantial, as if he has stepped out of some distant port or half-remembered voyage.

Around them, the atmosphere of the bar is hazy and dreamlike. A nickel-in-the-slot piano plays “Stamboul Nights,” its mechanical music drifting through the room and mingling with the man’s broken, wandering speech. The tune seems to blur the boundaries between the present moment and faraway places. As he talks, his words come in fragments—part confession, part memory, part delirium—so that the music, the alcohol, and the dim light all become inseparable from the story he is trying to tell.

The man speaks repeatedly of ships, of time, and of the urgency of departure. He insists that he must be “put out at three” for the S.S. Ala, a ship bound for Antwerp. This fixed appointment gives shape to his rambling, as though the whole world has narrowed to the hour of sailing and the need to be carried back to the sea. Time, for him, is not steady or ordinary; it seems broken into watches, departures, tides, and ports.

Gradually, he reveals a restless and wandering past. He has been whaling, worked a donkey engine in Panama, sold goods in Yucatan, and traveled along countless coasts. His life appears to have been spent in motion, moving from one difficult job to another, from one harbor to the next, never staying anywhere long enough to belong. The fragments of his biography suggest hardship, adventure, and exhaustion, but also a deep inability to remain still.

The passage as a whole blends memory, music, alcohol, and surreal imagery into a disorienting vision. Seas and cities rise and vanish in the man’s speech; the bar seems to open out onto distant oceans, tropical coasts, lava fields, and volcanic landscapes. Ordinary details become strange and unstable, transformed by the music of “Stamboul Nights” and the man’s feverish recollections. What begins as a meeting in a South Street bar becomes a dreamlike journey through ports, ships, heat, danger, and the restless imagination of a man who has lived too long among departures.

A fragmented urban encounter centers on a disoriented seafarer whose speech moves restlessly between the present city and the remembered spaces of his voyages. He appears as a man out of place: physically present in the street, yet mentally adrift among ships, docks, foreign ports, brutal labor, and the terrifying whiteness of the Arctic. Rather than offering a clear, orderly autobiography, he recounts his life in broken images and sudden associations. His memories surface as flashes—snatches of work at sea, glimpses of cold landscapes, fragments of violence, exhaustion, and fear. These details do not form a stable narrative; instead, they imitate the movement of a damaged mind struggling to organize experience.

The text uses stream-of-consciousness techniques to convey this instability. The seafarer’s thoughts shift abruptly from one moment to another, collapsing the distance between past and present. Overheard speech, urban noise, and repeated song fragments interrupt his recollections, creating the sense that his mind is full of echoes. These recurring phrases function almost like involuntary memories: they return without warning, suggesting experiences that cannot be fully understood or laid to rest. The songs and scattered voices give the passage a haunting rhythm, as if the man’s identity has been pieced together from labor chants, sailors’ talk, public conversation, and traumatic recollection.

His broken sense of time is central to the portrait. He does not seem to inhabit a continuous present. Instead, he drifts through overlapping layers of memory, where the sea, the city, and the Arctic coexist. The Arctic in particular becomes more than a geographical location; it represents extremity, isolation, and psychic damage. Its coldness and vastness seem to have entered the man’s inner life, leaving him emotionally frozen and estranged from ordinary human connection. Travel, which might conventionally suggest freedom or adventure, is presented here as a source of dislocation and suffering. The man has crossed distances, but those journeys have not enlarged or liberated him; they have fractured him.

As a result, the seafarer becomes a symbol of modern displacement. He embodies the experience of someone shaped by global movement, industrial labor, and violent encounter, yet unable to transform those experiences into a coherent story. His mind bears the marks of a world in which people are uprooted, used, and left psychologically wounded. The urban setting intensifies this condition: surrounded by voices and movement, he remains profoundly isolated. His speech reveals not mastery over experience, but damage by experience. Through his fragmented memories, recurring songs, and unstable perception of time, the text presents him as a figure of modern trauma—a man whose voyages have left him permanently adrift.

On the south side of town, there was a quiet street lined with old brick houses and tall trees that bent gently in the wind. Every morning, an elderly man named Thomas walked there with his small dog, greeting neighbors with a smile.

His favorite place was the corner where sunlight reached the pavement first. He said it reminded him of his childhood, when the south wind carried the smell of fresh bread from the bakery and the street was filled with laughter.

Though the town had changed over the years, that street remained special to him. It held his memories, his stories, and the simple peace of a place he had always called home.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense modernist prose-poem in the style of Hart Crane, set in a seedy waterfront bar on South Street, featuring a sailor rambling about Antwerp, Panama, Yucatan, Popocatepetl, the Arctic, and a nickel-slot piano playing “Stamboul Nights.”
counterfactuals.output:
In the tar-black gloss of South Street, where the river shouldered its barges like bruised commandments, the bar leaned seaward—one yellow tooth in a jaw of warehouses. Rain made a scripture of the windows. Under the cracked mirror, amid oyster-shell, spittle, brass, and the stale laurels of beer, the nickel-slot piano struck up “Stamboul Nights,” tinny as a crescent moon dropped in a cash-drawer, and its little hammers worried the dark with silk bazaars, false minarets, a eunuch’s laugh of treble wire.

There the sailor—cap listing, beard salted with the thaw of many latitudes—poured his voice across the table as though unloading contraband. Antwerp, he said, was bells in a fog, a cathedral’s bone-hand groping the Scheldt; and Panama, a green knife opening the earth while parrots screamed over fever and dredges, iron angels, gnawed the continental flesh. He had seen Yucatán whiten under noon like a skull lifted from jungle, temples stairing upward to a god gone off in thunder; had watched Popocatépetl—old smoking father—loosen at dusk a plume like burnt lace over the purple maize. And the Arctic, ah, the Arctic—there his words slowed, glassing over: a white saloon without doors, stars nailed low, the aurora spilling absinthe on the floes, and ships held fast as sins in a priest’s cold mouth.

Around him the bar breathed bilge, tobacco, cheap perfume, and drowned oranges. Dock-rats moved like punctuation in the corners. A woman in a red hat laughed once—then closed, a fan snapping shut. Outside, the East River dragged its chain of lights toward Brooklyn, toward morning’s gray indictment; inside, the piano’s mechanical heart spent nickel after nickel on Stamboul, Stamboul, that tarnished mirage rocking between continents, while the sailor’s hands opened and closed on nothing, hauling in rope from vanished harbors.

O South Street!—last gutter of empire, hymnbook soaked in rum—your lamps burn low over passports, knife-scars, cargo manifests, and the blue tattoos of men who have given their bodies to maps. In that bar, night gathered all oceans into one glass, and drank; and the sailor, still speaking, became a mast in smoke, a latitude of loss, his voice crossing Antwerp, Panama, Yucatán, Popocatépetl, the Arctic—until the tune ran down with a click, and silence came up from the river, black and shining, to claim its change.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental early-20th-century American monologue with fragmented syntax, maritime imagery, green light, drunken barroom music, and a worn-out ex-whaler talking about lost time and ships leaving at three.
counterfactuals.output:
Three o’clock, I told them. Three.

But the clock over the bottles had drowned years ago—stopped, maybe, in a storm, maybe in a fistfight—hands pointing nowhere, and the piano kept saying yes, yes, yes in that cracked saloon way, one tooth gone from every chord. A woman laughed into her beer. Somebody stamped. Outside the harbor was black and slick as stove-polish, except for that green light trembling out there on the end of the pier, or beyond it, or beyond all piers.

I seen lights like that.

Not meant for coming home. Meant for keeping men awake.

Once I had shoulders. Once I had a back the rope could bite and not draw complaint. We took whales south of ice, north of God, all day the sea heaving under us like a drunk beast with no floor to fall on. Blood warm in the scuppers. Fog low. Bells. Men singing because if they stopped singing they heard themselves thinking.

And time—listen—time was not these little brass ticks in a barroom clock. Time was sailcloth cracking at dawn. Time was the cry from the masthead. Time was the long pull, the iron struck, the line running out so fast it smoked and shrieked like a soul being paid away.

Then back to port. Always back. Or so we said.

The boys asked me, “Captain, when’s she leaving?”

Not captain now. Not anything now but Old Ben with salt in his knees and a hand that shakes before the glass touches it.

“Three,” I said.

Everything leaves at three. Ships, women, chances, youth. You think there’ll be another tide, and there is, only it is not yours. You think the harbor holds a place for you, a rope looped over a piling, a cup kept warm, a face at a window. But the tide takes inventory in the dark and finds you wanting.

Hear that cornet? Like a gull with gin in its crop. Hear the drum? That’s the engine of some steamer backing out, black smoke, white wake, name painted fresh as a lie. The piano man knows. He’s playing all the departures at once.

I was ashore one night in New Bedford—or was it Gloucester, or a place the map forgot after the railroad went through—and there was a girl with a green ribbon in her hair. Green as harbor fire. Green as the last star over water. I told her I’d come back rich with oil, with ambergris, with Spanish combs, with anything a girl might forgive.

The ship sailed at three.

Or she did.

Or I did.

Years lay down after that like nets. Tangled, stinking, full of small dead things. You cut one knot and find another. The sea keeps no calendar. A man comes back and the street is narrower, the old bar has a new mirror, the girl is a woman is a stone is a story told wrong by strangers. And still, far out, that green light. Blinking. Not promise. Not warning. Just there. A small drowned eye that won’t close.

Pour me another.

No, don’t pity. Pity’s for the young who still believe it changes weather.

I tell you there are ships below us now. Under these floorboards. Under the fiddles and spit and sawdust. Whole fleets sliding out on black water, sails filling with breath we wasted. You can feel them when the music stumbles. There—there—did you feel it? Keel passing under the bar. Cargo of lost mornings. Hold full of unsent letters. Men on deck with faces like mine before I wore it out.

Three o’clock.

The hour has a sound. Not bell, not whistle. More like a door softly closing in a room you thought was empty.

And the green light shakes on the water. Shakes and steadies. Shakes and steadies.

As if saying: almost.

As if saying: never.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a lyrical modernist passage about meeting a strange tall man with green glasses in a South Street tavern; include a recurring song refrain about “Stamboul Rose,” references to Leviathan, Plato, rum, the S.S. Ala, and volcanic ruins.
counterfactuals.output:
In a tavern on South Street, where the windows sweated salt and the lamps burned with a yellow, submarine patience, I met the tall man in green glasses.

He stood beside the bar as if he had been unloaded there from some foreign steamer—too long in the legs, too narrow in the face, his coat black and shining at the seams. Behind the smoked lenses his eyes were only rumors. He held a glass of rum but did not drink it. The fiddle in the corner was sawing at a tune the sailors knew, and every few measures the room leaned into the refrain:

*O Stamboul Rose, Stamboul Rose,*  
*where the black tide goes, nobody knows.*

He asked me whether I believed in Leviathan.

Not the whale, he said. Not the printed monster in a child’s Bible. The true Leviathan: that nation of hunger sleeping under the floorboards, under harbors, under names.

I said I had once read Plato and found the cave damp.

At this he smiled, or perhaps the green glasses merely altered the light. “Plato,” he said, “was a customs officer of shadows. He took the sun and stamped it with a seal.”

Outside, South Street rattled with drays, gulls, chains, the coppery shout of men rolling barrels toward the piers. Somewhere in the dark the S.S. Ala was taking on cargo—coffee, machinery, bolts of cloth, and one crate, he said, packed with ash from volcanic ruins. “Ruins still warm,” he whispered. “Cities that remember fire better than men remember love.”

The room sang again, softer now, as if the song had learned discretion:

*O Stamboul Rose, Stamboul Rose,*  
*red in the glass where the old moon shows.*

He told me he had come from an island where the church bells had melted in the eruption and run like tears into the square. He had seen stairs leading nowhere, a fountain full of pumice, a child’s tin soldier fused to a saint’s foot. “Volcanic ruins,” he said, “are the only honest architecture. They admit the world is temporary.”

He lifted the rum then, and the tavern seemed to lift with it—the bar, the fiddle, the battered mirrors, the faces of sailors pale as codfish under smoke. I saw us all as figures painted on the inside of a bottle: Plato drunk, Leviathan dreaming, the S.S. Ala groaning at her ropes, and the tall man with green glasses bending toward me like a mast in stormlight.

“What do you want?” I asked.

He answered by singing with the rest:

*O Stamboul Rose, Stamboul Rose,*  
*keep your name where the sea-wind blows.*

Then he was gone—not through the door, I think, but through some crack in the evening. His rum remained untouched. On the counter lay a pinch of gray ash and a scrap of paper with a map of no country I recognized.

All night the tavern breathed. All night South Street smelled of tar, oranges, bilge, and rain. And from the harbor, where the S.S. Ala waited like a thought too large for speech, there came a low sound—not foghorn, not engine, not tide exactly—but something vast turning over in its sleep.

*O Stamboul Rose, Stamboul Rose,*  
*down where the drowned green lantern glows.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Imitate the style of a 1920s modernist long poem: a narrator encounters a nervous sailor whose speech drifts through memories of whaling, Panama Canal work, Yucatan peddling, Arctic trauma, and a ship bound for Antwerp, with jagged punctuation and musical refrains.
counterfactuals.output:
At the lunch-room’s zinc, under the greenish clock,  
where flies made decimals of the sugar-bowl  
and the elevated iron coughed—coughed—  
I found him:  

a tarry wrist, a collar wilted to rope,  
eyes stitched wide by weather.  
He kept one hand upon his cup  
as if the coffee might depart without him.

“Listen—” he said, though I had not spoken,  
“the sea’s got hinges in it.  
You hear them nights.  Clank—clank—  
like lock-gates, like teeth—”

O blue! O bitter clarinet of foam!  
Sing ho, the derrick and the gull,  
sing low, the harbor’s iron lull—

He had been after whales, he told me,  
south of a moon white as a scraped bone,  
where the boats went out like splinters  
from the mother-ship’s black thumb.  
“Warm blood on water—slick—  
and the old bull sounding, sounding,  
taking all the stars down with him.  
We rowed in the dark.  God, how we rowed.  
The oars were ribs.  The ribs were ours.”

Then suddenly Panama—  
a red cut in the world, fever-steamed,  
men coughing gold into the mud,  
shovels ringing noon, night, noon,  
the jungle crowding close with green knives.  
“Canal?” he laughed.  “A scar, boy.  
A scar with ships walking through it.  
We dug till the hills remembered us,  
till dynamite said Amen—  
and mules slid backward in the rain.”

O blow, black whistle, over Gatun!  
O wheel, O chain, O drowned monsoon!  
Hi-yo, the locks lift up the moon—

His fingers tapped the counter:  
five small hammers in a coffin-shop.  
“I sold tin saints in Yucatán,  
needles, combs, bright cloth, blue thread,  
walking the white roads where the lizards blinked  
and the church-bells had dust in their throats.  
Women with maize-hands, children quiet as gourds—  
I’d cry my wares.  I’d cry, I’d cry—  
but parrots took my voice  
and hung it in the ceiba trees.”

The waitress leaned to hear; the spoons were still.  
Outside, a taxi’s horn split into brass petals.  
He flinched.

“North,” he whispered.  “Don’t say ice.  
Don’t say it.”

But ice entered anyway:  
pane upon pane in his stare,  
white knives sliding under the door of speech.  
A mast snapped.  A dog howled once.  
The sun went round and round, a coin no hand could spend.  
“We ate the boots.  We boiled the straps.  
One man sang hymns to his mother’s mitten.  
Another walked out to fetch dawn—  
kept walking—  
small—smaller—  
then the snow shut.”

O hush, white fiddle, thin and high!  
O frost in the beard, O nail in the sky!  
No harbor answers when the dead go by—

He drank; the cup rang against his teeth.  
“Antwerp,” he said, and smiled at no one.  
“There’s a ship tonight—smoke already in her lungs.  
She’ll nose past buoys, past Staten’s lamps,  
past the last red wink of the channel—  
then open water, then gulls gone,  
then Europe like a rumor under fog.  
Antwerp!  Bells in the rain, beer-dark windows,  
cobbles shining like seal-backs.  
Maybe I’ll sleep there.  Maybe.”

The clock jumped.  
The elevated flung its shadowed vertebrae  
across the panes.  
In his pocket coins chimed—little anchors—  
and far off, or near, a siren braided the dusk.

“Don’t follow the water,” he told me.  
“It follows back.”

Then he rose with the delicate care  
of a man lifting a sleeping child,  
buttoned the sea inside his coat,  
and went out—  
past neon, ash-cans, newspaper boys,  
past the fish-stink wharves and the ropes’ wet grammar—  
toward a funnel smoking for Antwerp.

O blue! O bitter clarinet of foam!  
Sing ho, the derrick and the gull—  
the sailor walks; the tide walks home;  
the city tilts its iron skull.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal nautical bar scene as a stream-of-consciousness prose poem, using abrupt dashes, repeated colors and sounds, a nickel piano, a drunken sailor’s fractured travel stories, and ominous images of the sea, lava, skeleton cities, and green drowning drums.
counterfactuals.output:
The bar leans sideways in the rain—blue rain, black rain, blue—its windows sweating salt and lamplight, its floorboards breathing like old whales, and in the corner the nickel piano keeps coughing out tin roses—plink, clank, plink—five cents for a memory, five cents for a shipwreck, five cents for the moon to fall into your glass.

The sailor at the counter has one eye full of harbor fog and one eye full of lava. He says he has been to Lisbon—no, Java—no, the red canal under the earth where the fish have human teeth and sing hymns backward. He says, Pour me the green one, the green-green one, the one that sounds like drums under water. The bartender pours, and the liquid knocks—boom, boom, boom—against the glass like drowning.

Outside, the sea lifts its black head.

Inside, everyone pretends not to notice.

The sailor laughs—ha, ha, broken gull—then spills a map from his mouth: I saw a city made of skeletons, he says, white streets, white towers, white birds with no feathers—Paris, maybe, or Port Said, or my mother’s kitchen after the tide came in. The nickel piano jingles blue-blue-blue, its yellow teeth striking little hammers at the dark. Smoke crawls up the walls like squid ink. Rum smells of copper. The lamps swing though there is no wind.

I remember—he says—I remember a volcano walking beside our ship, its mouth full of orange bells, its feet melting the deck, and the captain prayed to a compass that pointed only down. Down, down, down. The crew turned green in their sleep. Green hands, green tongues, green dreams. Then came the drums—dull drums, drowned drums, green drowning drums—booming from beneath the hull as if the ocean had a heart too large and sick to keep.

Someone drops a coin.

The piano shivers.

Plink—clank—plunk—blue.

Now the bar is floating, perhaps it always was, stools nailed to a tide, bottles bobbing behind the mirror where another sea waits with its mouth open. The sailor’s beard is full of tiny anchors. His boots leak stars. He whispers that every port is the same port if you arrive drunk enough, every woman a lighthouse, every lighthouse a bone, every bone a mast picked clean by black weather.

Red-red lava in the ashtray.

Green-green drums in the floor.

White-white skeleton cities rising in the foam.

And the sea—hush, hush, hush—the sea pressing its cold face to the door, asking for credit, asking for a song, asking which of us will go first.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
